title: Priority-aware admission controller for Dedicated GPU pools
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem summary:
Customers using Redwood Dedicated report unpredictable tail latency and silent token-cost spikes during multi-tenant bursts. Current Dedicated routing only uses coarse per-pool concurrency limits and autoscaler capacity. We need an admission controller at the routing edge for Dedicated GPU pools that combines per-tenant and per-route rate limits, bounded queueing with priority lanes, and SLO-driven overload shedding. The controller should collaborate with the autoscaler and fleet controller to provide throughput guarantees while protecting high-priority customers and preventing noisy neighbors from degrading global SLOs.

Goal:
- Implement a configurable admission controller that: applies per-tenant and per-route token-bucket rate limits; maintains bounded queues with priority lanes and fair share; performs graceful overload shedding based on latency and queue thresholds; emits metrics and tracing for every admission decision; and exposes knobs for product (P0/P1 tiers) and runtime to express priority and cost trade-offs.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for long-term model routing policies (e.g., model downgrade to smaller quantized variants). Not tackling billing/reporting changes in this ticket (separate PM work).
acceptance_criteria: Edge admission layer enforces per-tenant and per-route rate limits (token-bucket) configurable per Dedicated pool.
Two-level bounded queue implemented: priority lane (P0/P1) and best-effort lane, with a global max-queue-per-worker metric and per-tenant caps.
Overload shedding triggers when latency P95 > configured SLO or queue depth exceeds threshold; shedding decisions logged and include reason code.
Autoscaler integrations: admission controller exposes headroom signals and a pending-request gauge consumed by the autoscaler to scale up earlier.
Comprehensive metrics and traces emitted (admit/queue/reject/drop, per-tenant rate, queue latency), and dashboards created in Grafana playbook.
E2E test harness simulates noisy neighbor and burst traffic; high-priority traffic retains >=90% of throughput when under strain in the sim environment.
Feature flag rollout path and canary plan documented for gradual enablement in dedicated pools.
Security review completed and perf regression within 5% tail latency overhead at nominal load.
design_notes: Admission model: hierarchical token buckets — global pool allowance -> per-tenant bucket -> per-route bucket. Token refill rates derive from dedicated pool committed throughput and customer SLA.

Queueing: implement two FIFO queues per worker process: priority and best-effort. Priority queue ingress allowed up to a ratio (default 80% of queue slots). Use weighted fair-queueing at worker when multiple tenants present.

Shedding policy: multi-stage: 1) reject best-effort when queue depth exceeds 70% or P95 latency > SLO; 2) probabilistic shedding for top offenders when sustained overload; 3) preemptive rejection of low-priority long-running requests to protect short interactive ones.
Autoscaler coupling: publish 'pending_requests' and 'admission_utilization' metrics. Autoscaler can use moving-average of pending_requests to trigger scale-up before queue saturation.
Rate limits: token-bucket windows support bursts. Per-tenant windows computed from tenant commit + safety margin. Provide admin override for emergency traffic prioritization.
Compatibility: admission controller implemented as a middleware in the routing layer so it applies to Hosted and Dedicated but with Dedicated-specific config exposed in the Dedicated control plane.

Data and observability: every admission decision writes a minimal decision event to the internal event stream (tenant_id, route, decision_code, queue_time_ms, pool_id) to power dashboards and post-incident analysis.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (Spike, 1w): prototype token-bucket + priority queue in a sidecar mock and measure tail overhead using synthetic workload generator. Create confluence doc with design diagrams.
Phase 2 (Core impl, 2w): implement admission middleware in routing service, integrate token store, add metrics and tracing. Add feature flag gating per pool.
Phase 3 (Autoscaler integration, 1w): surface headroom/pending metrics and add autoscaler hook to consider pending_requests in scale decisions.
Phase 4 (Testing & canary, 1w): run e2e noisy-neighbor scenarios against dedicated staging clusters; create Grafana dashboards and alert rules.
Phase 5 (Rollout, 1w): enable for low-volume dedicated pools, monitor for regressions, incrementally open to higher-volume pools after two business days of stable metrics.
test_plan: Unit tests for token-bucket correctness and queue admission logic.
Integration tests that validate priority lanes and preemption behavior under synthetic bursts.
Chaos tests that simulate worker slowdowns and confirm shedding decisions and autoscaler reactions.
Performance benchmark comparing tail latency with admission off vs on at 100% and 130% nominal load.
Regression test that verifies no request is admitted without audit logging when flag is enabled.
risks: Risk of added latency from admission checks on the hot path — mitigate with optimized in-memory token cache and fast-path admit for most requests.
Incorrect bucket sizing may starve tenants or allow noisy neighbors — require conservative defaults and an admin override path.
Autoscaler feedback loops if signals are noisy — use moving averages and dampening to avoid oscillation.
Shedding may cause customer-visible 429s; need clear comms and gradual rollout.
